payload.source_label: A constant-coefficient system is hyperbolic when A has real eigenvalues and m linearly independent eigenvectors

contract.statement: For the one-dimensional homogeneous linear system q_t + A q_x = 0, where q takes values in R^m and A is a constant real m × m matrix, hyperbolicity is defined by A admitting a full real eigenvector basis with real associated eigenvalues. Relative to any such selected basis, every vector in R^m has unique expansion coefficients. The eigenvalues are the propagation speeds of the corresponding wave components. The source imposes no distinctness or sign restriction on those eigenvalues and does not restrict the definition to the motivating two-component acoustics example. Sources: raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, equation (1.1) and its description; raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening defining paragraph; raw PDF pages 69–70, printed pages 47–48, equations (3.2)–(3.6) and their explanations. The treatment of dimension zero is not explicit in these passages.
assumptions: The system being classified is the homogeneous, first-order, one-dimensional, constant-coefficient linear system (1.1); raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, text introducing (1.1), and raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, defining sentence.
Its coefficient matrix A is real and square of size m × m; raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, description immediately following (1.1).

The selected definition inherits the real state space and real coefficient matrix from the earlier introduction of (1.1); it is not a definition over an arbitrary scalar field. Locations: raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, description following (1.1); raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, explicit reference back to (1.1).

The acoustic example preceding the definition motivates its wave interpretation but supplies no additional assumptions on the general matrix A. Locations: raw PDF page 24, printed page 2, equations (1.5)–(1.6); raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, transition from two acoustic equations to the general definition.

The defining paragraph introduces no initial data, boundary conditions, or regularity hypothesis on q as part of the matrix criterion. Its classification refers directly to A's eigenstructure. Location: raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, defining sentence.

The Chapter 3 cross-reference explains the decomposition promised in the selected paragraph. The explicit reduction to decoupled equations there uses constancy of A. Locations: raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, Chapter 3 cross-reference; raw PDF page 69, printed page 47, equations (3.1)–(3.3) and the warning immediately after (3.3).
quantifiers: The dimension m is the number of unknown components and the size of the square matrix A; the source introduces q: R × R → R^m and A as m × m in the paragraph following (1.1), raw PDF page 23, printed page 1.
A is a fixed real matrix of size m × m, constant with respect to the independent space and time variables; raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, description following (1.1).
The independent variables are x and t, and q(x,t) is an R^m-valued unknown in q_t + A q_x = 0; raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, equation (1.1) and its surrounding paragraph.

A mathematical unpacking of the defining existence claim uses real numbers lambda^p and vectors r^p in R^m, indexed by p = 1,...,m. The selected paragraph requires m corresponding eigenvectors; Chapter 3 uses this indexing and identifies them as right eigenvectors. Locations: raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening paragraph; raw PDF page 69, printed page 47, equation (3.2); raw PDF page 70, printed page 48, equation (3.6).

The unique-decomposition consequence universally quantifies over every vector v in R^m, with the eigenvector family already fixed; raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, sentence beginning 'This means that any vector'.
